overview: These entries follow Milan through Spanish and Austrian government, with the last Sforza years at the beginning of the earlier map interval. They are phases of a changing territorial state, not two unrelated civilizations. Its surviving hospital, theatre, libraries and printed books show care, work and argument alongside imperial rule.

periods.title: From Sforza to Spanish government
periods.summary: Francesco II Sforza died in 1535. Milan subsequently formed part of the Spanish monarchy’s Italian possessions; 1530 is the atlas’s coverage boundary.

periods.title: Austrian Milan
periods.summary: Austrian rule began in 1706, with wartime interruptions and major administrative changes. The later Milano Austria entry samples this phase.

periods.title: French conquest and new governments
periods.summary: French forces displaced Austrian government in 1796. The map’s Austrian label extending to 1800 is an imprecise interval, not continuous control by one ruler.

items.text: Milan’s great hospital, the Ca’ Granda, had been founded in 1456, before these map intervals. Its foundation ceremony included small vessels of oil, wine, milk, honey and water and a lead book. These were symbolic deposits, not a recipe for treating patients.

The Ca’ Granda’s buildings grew over roughly three centuries, helped by citizens’ gifts and bequests. The recurring Festa del Perdono raised support. Hospital care depended on lasting institutions and donors, not simply on a duke paying for one impressive building and walking away.

The hospital placed latrines in corridors beside the wards. Channels supplied with rainwater helped carry waste away. Convenient toilets were part of the architectural plan centuries before modern hospital plumbing; surviving remains have also been altered, so today’s building is not an untouched fifteenth-century snapshot.

Wastewater from the hospital passed under the Naviglio canal and toward agricultural land used for irrigation and fertilizing. That is evidence of engineered drainage and reuse, not proof of modern sewage treatment or protection from infection. The unglamorous pipes deserve a place beside the grand courtyards.

A courtyard originally associated with baths was used for servants and nurses by the early seventeenth century. Such changing uses remind us that a hospital needed workers and service spaces as well as beds. The elegant architecture was also somebody’s workplace.

A new assessment of Milanese taxable wealth was completed in 1560. Officials sought to distribute costs, but urban and rural interests and existing privileges complicated the process. A government’s demand for money reached farms and households, even when its records speak in the language of institutions.

The Sforza Castle became a barracks during foreign rule. Its changing function is a reminder that a former prince’s residence could become a military workplace. Spanish, Austrian and French rulers reused the same formidable building rather than rebuilding Milan from scratch after every conquest.

Brera’s art collection began in 1776 in connection with the academy, giving students examples to study. Its formal museum opened in 1809, after this Austrian phase. Many later additions came from suppressed religious houses: a museum’s collection can preserve the effects of political upheaval.

After the Jesuit establishment passed to the state in 1773, Brera gathered learning institutions in one complex, including an observatory, botanical garden and library. The Braidense library opened to the public in 1786. Books, plants and the sky became neighboring subjects of investigation.

La Scala opened in 1778 with Salieri’s Europa riconosciuta, replacing a theatre destroyed by fire. Maria Theresa authorized the new building, designed by Giuseppe Piermarini. Its name preserves the church formerly on the site; the audience was entering a newly constructed theatre, not an ancient Roman one.

La Scala’s boxes had owners whose names can be traced in archival records beginning in 1778. An evening at the theatre was also a social occasion shaped by property and status. The records illuminate the people who held boxes, not a representative sample of every Milanese family.

The Italian title “Dei delitti e delle pene” means “On Crimes and Punishments.” A surviving 1764 edition preserves these words from Cesare Beccaria’s famous argument about criminal justice. The Milanese author published in Livorno; a book could travel across political borders faster than a government changed its laws.

ending.text: French conquest in 1796 ended this phase of Austrian government and brought new political arrangements. Milan remained inhabited and important. Neither the 1715 endpoint of the first map entry nor the 1800 endpoint of the later one is a reliable single date for the city’s “fall.”
